speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: HEAVY WATER-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SITE OF SECOND PLANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that on June 14 last I informed the house that Canadian General Electric Company Limited had been granted an extension to June 30 for selection of the site for the heavy water plant to be constructed by that company.
I am now informed by CGE that the site selected is on the Cape Breton side of the strait of Canso in the province of Nova Scotia. An overriding factor in favour of this site was the deuterium content in the water that will be used in the manufacturing process.
A power plant, fuelled with oil with provision for backing up with coal, will be built by the Nova Scotia power commission to supply steam and electric power for the heavy water plant. It is hoped that in time these plants will be part of a larger industrial complex in Cape Breton in line with this government's concern to find new industries for the Atlantic provinces, industries based on modern technology and modern forms of energy.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare, who has been closely associated with the Minister of Finance and myself in this matter, rejoices in this announcement. I am sure the members representing the province of Nova Scotia in this house, the premier and the government of Nova Scotia will also share fully in these sentiments.

speechtext:
Hear, hear.

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-217, to amend the Criminal Code (publication of ingredients of wonder drugs).

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF DRUG INGREDIENTS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF DRUG INGREDIENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the object of this bill is to prevent a recurrence of such incidents as the public announcement in the press claiming curative action of an anti-cancer hormone, coupled with the refusal to divulge the ingredients thereof. Such premature announcement has caused great mental anguish, not only to those afflicted with the disease but also to members of their families. This bill would make it a criminal offence for anyone to make public pronouncements or to call press conferences claiming cures for dread diseases without first divulging all the ingredients of the formula to the National Research Council, where proper and adequate tests can be made.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, June 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mac-Eachen for the second reading of Bill No. C-207, to authorize the making of contributions by Canada toward the cost of programs for the provision of assistance and welfare services to and in respect of persons in need.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislation now before the house contains the long awaited Canada Assistance Plan. For over a year the people of Canada, particularly the old age pensioners, have been told with a great fanfare of trumpets and clanging of cymbals that the arrival of the Canada Assistance Plan would solve all their problems. Now we have the plan before us and I must say it is a pathetic response to a great social need. One would almost be justified in using the old and hackneyed phrase that the mountain has laboured and brought forth a mouse.
Not only are the old age pensioners and the public generally disappointed in this legislation but there is a growing indication that many backbenchers on the government side of the house are equally disappointed. Last night it was an interesting spectacle to watch some of the ministers flitting like butterflies from member to member on the government side, trying to persuade them to refrain from

Canada Assistance Plan taking part in the debate and assuring them that if they would just wait until the minister spoke their worst fears would be assuaged.
The government has even become so desperate that it has now started a rumour that the minister is going to make some pronouncement that will relieve the concern of the old age pensioners. If the government feels that concurrently with the old age assistance plan there ought to be legislation to increase the old age security pension, the minister had ample opportunity to announce that when he brought in this legislation.
Further, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) had ample opportunity yesterday when the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) specifically asked him if the government would bring down legislation to raise the pension to $100 a month before there was a summer adjournment, but the Prime Minister brushed that aside. Today the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) has had ample opportunity, either on motions or during the question period, to announce a policy that would give some hope to our older citizens that the government has not quite forgotten them.
If the minister is prepared to indicate that before we recess for the summer he will bring down concurrent legislation providing $100 a month to old age security pensioners at age 65, he has only to nod his head and I am quite prepared to sit down and give him the floor. But I am not prepared to fall for the old ruse of allowing the minister to close the debate and prevent members on this side of the house from expressing their opinions, on the supposition that he is going to do something, when all the record of the past indicates that the government is not likely to do very much.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
In the first place, I wish to say that the Canada Assistance Plan is good administrative legislation. It will do many things which social welfare workers have been advocating over the years. First of all, it will remove many of the restrictive categories and will enable welfare workers to deal with individuals as people rather than as statistics in a given category. In this way it will provide a flexibility for welfare workers which they have not enjoyed in the past. Certainly in the matter of administering welfare programs this is a forward step.
This plan substitutes a needs test in place of a means test. This also has some advantages. One advantage is that where a provincial government is generous and where the

June 30. 1966
Canada Assistance Plan welfare worker is trained it will enable those administering the welfare programs to supply whatever funds are necessary to meet the special need of a particular case. That is something welfare workers have been asking for a long time. It is very difficult when bureaucrats lay down circumscribed conditions and maximum figures of allowable income or the amount of the grant which can be given to deal with special cases. A person may have diabetes and need insulin or a special diet. He may require a hearing aid. There is a whole host of things such as home care and special training that cannot be foreseen in the preparation of regulations which are necessary to give the welfare worker sufficient elbow room so that he or she can deal with special cases of need.
It should be pointed out at the same time that the needs test also has some distinct disadvantages. Where the provincial government is niggardly and where the welfare administrator is stingy the recipient can be worse off than he or she was before. The difficulty about a needs test is that it is a matter of subjective judgment. The concept of need is in the mind of the administrator. Consequently it is going to be difficult to exercise any uniformity of standards. Undoubtedly there will be different concepts of need as one goes from community to community and particularly as one goes from province to province. This causes me some concern, because unfortunately there has always been a disparity between the welfare benefits paid in the "have" provinces and those paid in the "have not" provinces.
One of the ideas inherent in an old age security pension as of right is that all Canadian citizens are entitled to the same amount of payment in their old age irrespective of where they live in Canada. I am concerned lest in relying upon a needs test without any standard of uniformity the "have" provinces can be fairly generous but the "have not" provinces, irrespective of how generous they may want to be, since they must match any payment they get from the federal government, may be required because of financial stringency to be much less generous than some of the more wealthy provinces. I cannot imagine anything which will contribute more to national disunity than to have a wide and growing disparity between the treatment of old people, widows, the crippled, the blind and the disabled, from province to province with less generous treatment in the poorer provinces than in the richer.

In my view the basic weakness in the Canada Assistance Plan is that it is wedded to the old concept of welfare. Assistance is still going to be granted on the basis of requiring each individual to pass a test. It is true it is to be a needs test rather than a means test, but it is still a test. It is an affront to human dignity to ask people because they are in bad financial circumstances to degrade and humiliate themselves by submitting to a test. What the government really is saying in this legislation is: We are going to help the needy people of Canada provided they are on their knees. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is little value in feeding the bodies of men and women if we are going to leave them with a sense of humiliation.
Last Sunday afternoon while I was attending a picnic in the city of Hamilton a longtime resident of that community walking with a cane hobbled up to me and said, "I want you to tell Mr. Pearson that I would rather starve than pass a test." I think he represents the view of hundreds of thousands of proud-spirited people in this country who are not going to submit themselves to a test and who feel, as a result of having toiled all their lives in helping to build Canada and bring it to what it is today, that they are entitled to the amenities of life without having to undergo an individual test.
The whole concept of welfare is changing throughout the world. In the United Kingdom at the present time legislation has been introduced to provide for a guaranteed annual income. In the United States a number of congressional and state committees are studying the same proposition, only they call it a negative income tax. Whatever terminology one may use, I am convinced we shall see public opinion in the years ahead force whatever government is in office to abolish the means test and the needs test and guarantee people in necessitous circumstances an income which can be determined by means of the income tax so that the individual will be assured that if whatever pension and income he has are not sufficient to meet a given minimum the government will make up the difference.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
We in the New Democratic Party feel that if the government were to establish $100 per month pensions at age 65 and set up a guaranteed annual income measure providing, let us say, $1,500 per year for single people and $3,000 per year for a married couple, people who had nothing but their
June 30, 1966

pensions would still be entitled to some additional assistance under the guaranteed annual income measure. Those who have some private income in addition to their pensions, and this would be indicated when they filed their income tax returns, would not be entitled to any additional payment.
This would not rule out the need for the Canada Assistance Plan. There will still be cases of special need and there will still be instances where welfare departments will have to step in because of special circumstances and give additional aid over and above any assistance that may be provided as a result of old age security pensions and guaranteed annual incomes.
The tragic thing about this legislation is that it really does nothing for the elderly citizens of Canada. The groups who are affected, recipients of mothers' allowances, the blind and disabled, need all the help they can get and that is why I should like to see the adoption of a guaranteed annual income measure. These people need more help than can be provided now and, in some provinces, more than the provinces can afford to pay. There is nothing in this legislation which will help the people who are trying to survive on $75 per month.
I consider this legislation the cruelest hoax that has ever been perpetrated on senior citizens of this country because their expectations were built up by the government and by the Liberal party. I could bring in stacks of Liberal campaign literature which informed the old people of the great assistance they were going to get when the Canada Assistance Plan was a^noted. For over a year every time we raised the question of increasing old age pensions we were told to wait until the Canada Assistance Plan was brought before the house. There is nothing in this legislation that will guarantee any assistance to the old age security pensioner. This measure does provide that if the provincial governments want to give additional money the federal government will pay part of the cost, but there is no guarantee that provincial governments will want to pay more and there are many provinces which may not be able to pay more.
What were the old people told about this Canada Assistance Plan? I have here the Toronto Star of October 16, 1965 which has a three-column, one-inch type heading reading "Pearson Pledges $100 A Month For Needy Old People". The article then states:
The government plans to pay pensions of more than $100 a month to old people with no other income, Prime Minister Pearson said last night.
Canada Assistance Plan
The article goes on to state:
The Liberals proposed to concentrate higher pensions on people who need more than $75 a month and have no other income.
The article then quotes the Prime Minister as stating:
Anybody who has only $75 from the state, and no other source of income, and needs more, even if it's $125-more than $100-should be in a position to get it.
It's so simple to say, "all right, you gave them $75, we'll give them $100". But I'm not going to engage in any auction of the people's money for that kind of thing.
Mr. Pearson did not estimate how much the proposed "Canada assistance program" would cost.
He said only that his government is prepared to pay "a large share" of the extra pensions-leaving the rest of the bill to the provinces.
The Ottawa Journal of the same date carried an article under the heading "Pledges Pension Boost" and the subheading "Pearson Promises $100 Or More For Needy Aged". Every other newspaper in the country carried similar stories. Many of the old age pensioners took the government's promise seriously, that if they had no other pension than $75 a month they would be entitled to $125 a month. That is the kind of propaganda that was spread, but there is nothing in this bill which will guarantee them a five cent piece more than the $75 a month they are getting right now.
I accuse the government of a cruel deception upon the old people of this country. I accuse the government of playing politics with the hopes and expectations which they aroused in the senior citizens of this country. Having built up great expectations by advance publicity the government is now trying to hurry this legislation through the house by introducing it late, hoping thereby that they can get it passed before the public becomes aware of the fact that the old people of this country have been betrayed and deceived. With respect to old age security pensioners this plan is a deliberate attempt to foist off on the provinces a responsibility which belongs to the government of Canada.
In 1951 the government of Canada asked for a constitutional amendment to give it exclusive jurisdiction in the matter of providing old age security pensions and it got that authority. What is more, it got the tax revenue to provide these pensions through a 4 per cent surcharge on personal income tax, 3 per cent on sales tax and 3 per cent on corporation tax. That money has gone into the old age security fund and it is quite a fund today. It has a surplus now in the neighbourhood of

June 30, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan $250 million and it is going up at the rate of $20 million a month. It is estimated that by March 31 next the fund will have a surplus of $455 million.
The government can well afford to make some additional payment to the old age pensioners. It may be that it is delaying this in order to use it as an election gimmick during the next campaign. I do not know if that is the intention, but if so it is a terrible way to treat the old people of this country. Instead of exercising the jursidiction which the government asked for and instead of spending the money it has taxed for this purpose, what is the government doing? It is now saying that $75 per month is all it is going to pay old age security pensioners.
The old age security pensioners need more. The Prime Minister said in a television interview during the last election campaign that they might need up to $125 a month. The government now says that if they need more let the provinces put it up and the government will pay half. There is no reason why the provinces should pay any part of this increase because these people are the exclusive responsibility of the government of Canada. The provinces have plenty of other responsibilities. They have all the rest of the welfare field lying at their doorstep and have inadequate financial resources, particularly in the have-not provinces.
This government has no excuse whatsoever for trying to shift part of its responsibility for looking after old age security pensioners on to the shoulders of provincial governments. There can be no doubt that the federal government can afford to increase these pensions to $100 per month, particularly in view of the surpluses that are building up in the old age security fund.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I hope the minister will not follow the line that has been followed by the Prime Minister on some occasions, namely, of pointing out that inflationary pressures would build up if we increased the old age pension. The old age pensioners are in a very anomalous position. When we are in a deflationary phase in the business cycle we do not give them an increase because we cannot afford it. When we are in an inflationary phase in the business cycle we cannot give them an increase because it will cause inflationary pressure. So the old age pensioners cannot win. If the government is convinced-I am not-that there is too much money chasing too few goods and that somebody's purchasing power

must be curtailed, the last people who ought to have their purchasing power curtailed are the elderly citizens of this country.

speechtext:
These are the people who need every dollar they can get just in order to live. Like all members of parliament I get letters from people all across this country. Here is one that came to me from the city of Toronto from a woman of 74 years of age who has been a widow for 10 years, is a diabetic and is partly crippled as a result. There is one phrase in this letter that has stayed with me ever since I read it. I could not get it out of my mind. She says:
I do hope and pray we will get a raise this month as I know I get hungry at times and I guess we all do. We will hope and pray for a brighter future.
When I think of a woman 74 years of age having to say "I get hungry at times" in a country that has the second highest standard of living in the world, a country that is in a state of affluence, a country whose gross national product has been increasing steadily throughout the years, it is certainly a reflection upon the adequacy of our social security program.
The argument which is being put up by members opposite, not by their speeches because they have been very careful not to make speeches but by their interjections, was expressed very well yesterday by the hon. member for High Park (Mr. Cameron) as reported at page 7076 of Hansard when he interrupted and asked a question. He said:
Like all members of the house I have a problem about which I want to ask him a very simple question. It is this. Rather than require pensioners to show a reasonable need, does the hon. member support the principle that we should pay the extra $25 a month to hundreds of thousands of people who do not require it at all?
Another member across the way interrupted yesterday to say, "Do you think that we should pay a pension to a person with an income of $10,000 a year?" Mr. Speaker, in the first place we thought this type of argument had ended long ago when parliament decided to set up an old age security pension without a means test and to pay it as a matter of right.
What about the question of paying this pension to people who do not really need it? First of all, how many are there? I think the figures show that of the people 70 years of age or over in this country the number with an income of $10,000 or over is 1.1 per cent.
June 30, 1966

We have to ask ourselves: Is it better to make 99 per cent of the people go through the humiliation of a test lest we pay too much to the 1 per cent? I would also remind the house that even the 1 per cent who may not need the pension have through the years paid their income tax surcharge and the 3 per cent sales tax into the old age security fund and are entitled to the pension. They have paid for it; it is not charity.

We in the New Democratic Party take the position that it is better to recover by means of income tax from the few who have too much rather than humiliate the many who have too little. We had hoped that the type of argument advanced by the hon. member for High Park and others, namely, that we cannot give everybody an increase in the pension because somebody who does not need it may receive it, had disappeared long ago.
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, we want a guaranteed annual income on a negative income tax basis. We want to see the end of tests. What the government is proposing here is that the old age pensioners will get $75 a month as of right. But anything more they get they will get by virtue of passing a test and on the basis of the generosity of the provincial government, and then the federal government will come in and pay part of the cost. I say that the government's failure to announce concurrent legislation, along with the Canada Assistance Plan, to raise the old age security pension is a betrayal of the people's hopes. We are not opposed to the Canada Assistance Plan. We do not object to what is in it. We are profoundly disappointed about what is not in it and the provision it does not make for the people who were led to believe that the Canada Assistance Plan would be the charter of their salvation.
I say that the Canadian people, when they realize the full implications of the government's neglect of our elderly citizens, will rise in their wrath and condemn this government. After all, the cost of living, which is bothering every family in Canada, falls just as heavily on the old people. In many ways it falls more severely on the old people because while in the last 12 months the weighted cost of living index for all commodities went up 4
Canada Assistance Plan per cent, if one takes the specific commodities which people must buy in order to live, food, clothing and shelter, those items have gone up more than 4 per cent. Consequently the cost of living for these old people has gone up to a very marked degree.
When the workers find that the cost of living is going up faster than their wages they have trade unions in many cases and can do something about it. They can negotiate a new agreement; or they can go out on strike if they want to. When farmers are pushed too far they can wheel their tractors out on the road. But these old people have no weapons with which to fight in the economic jungle of our modern society. They have nothing to appeal to except the conscience of the Canadian people, and I believe that the conscience of the Canadian people will be touched as they realize the full implications of the government's neglect. I am convinced that the backbenchers on the government side have had their consciences touched. I am convinced that if the government were to allow a free vote today on whether the old age pension should be raised to $100 a month at age 65, the motion would pass. Only the government's intransigence has kept them from passing it now.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I listened in particular to the comments made yesterday by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) and I can only come to the conclusion that the government's arrogance has dulled their sensibilities. When the Minister of Transport said yesterday that we have the best social security system in the world he certainly proved either that he does not know what he is talking about or that he has become so completely insulated from the people of this country that he has returned to the arrogance of 1957. Because any person who will look at the social security systems of some of the other countries of the world would not make the kind of statement that was made by the Minister of Transport. I invite the Minister of Transport to go out and tell the old age pensioners of this country, who are trying to eke out an existence on $75 a month, that we have the best social security system in the world-let him try telling them that and see what their reaction will be.
I think the government should stop and take stock. They are in a minority position in this house. They have stayed in office for the very obvious reason that no party today wants to put this country to the cost of another general election. So the government

Canada Assistance Plan has been given a free hand in bringing down legislation and has obtained the co-operation of all parties of this house in proceeding with their program.
I want to tell the government that unless they do something about the plight of old age pensioners, the opposition parties in this parliament will be justified in combining and putting this government out of office. I think the people of Canada would support them in taking such a step. After all, the last time the Liberal government was defeated was in 1957, and the reason for its defeat was that it had become so arrogant that it lost touch with the feelings and the social conscience of the Canadian people. Despite the fact that they had a large surplus in the treasury, the very best they could do was to raise the old age pension by $6 a month. When opposition members of that day raised their voices in protest, they received the same kind of answers that we have been getting these past two or three days.
But when the government-dubbed as the "six bucks boys"-went to the people in the election of 1957 they found that the reaction of the Canadian people was such as to put them out of office. I suggest they would be wise not to make the same mistake again. The Canadian people are patient and long suffering but their patience is wearing thin. The great bulk of the Canadian people, concerned as they are about their own problem of getting sufficient income to meet the rising cost of living, are also concerned about their neighbours and their fellow Canadians. There is hardly a community in Canada in which there are not old people who are in need, and these people have touched the conscience of their neighbours and their friends.
I want to tell the government that the Canadian people will not put up too long with a government that refuses to take the steps which are so obvious and to use the money which is now available in the old age security fund to provide these old people with some of the amenities and decencies of life. If this government wants to put some muscle into its war on poverty, here is the place to begin.
Let them begin by bringing in concurrent legislation so that in addition to the Canada Assistance Plan the old age security pensioners of this country will get $100 a month, not by passing a test, not by having to depend on a generous provincial government, but by right, and by virtue of the fact that this parliament has made it clear that it will live

up to its federal responsibilities for the elderly people of Canada.

I usually do not intervene in debates in this house on social and economic subjects, Mr. Speaker, the reason being that I have been assigned certain other responsibilities. However, I feel that if I did not intervene in this particular debate I would be derelict in my duty, particularly my duty to my constituents. I know of no single subject upon which my constituents are more concerned than the subject which is being discussed in this debate. On no single subject have I had more letters, more sincere and moving letters. I imagine this is true of every member in the house. I am not forgetting the fact that when I went around to seek election, as other members did, I called upon many people in the constituency and person after person urged me, if I did anything in this house, I should do my best to work toward an increase in the old age pension.
Such oratory as I have, Mr. Speaker, is not of the tear jerking variety. I do not propose to try to put into rhetorical terms the situation that faces many of my constituents, who are typical of people all across Canada. However, I want to read one or two letters which were brought to my attention and which set out typical situations about which we have heard. I quote:
I am going to be 80 years old In a few months and I have been receiving the old age pension since the age of 65.
The money I am receiving from the pension is not enough to keep me going, Mr. Brewin. I've needed new glasses for one year now and I am not able to buy them. Because of this I am not able to read and my eyes bum terribly.
Canada Assistance Plan
The doctor informs me that I also have a hernia.
I need medicine at times, and I cannot buy it. I have no other income but my pension.
I am not eating properly since I must be extremely frugal in order to survive.
People have told me to write to you, Mr. Brewin, and they said you would help me to receive $100 or $104.
I do not believe it would be a very fair answer to this person if I were to say that, well, some time in the future we may be going to do something about this or if I were to say, well, the weather is getting hot, the government is anxious to have a recess, at a time when we have an opportunity to speak up for these people as a result of this debate. If I were concerned about matters of that sort, if I were worried because somebody said I was filibustering or taking up time unnecessarily, I believe I would be failing in my duty if I did not bring these matters to the attention of the house.
I have another letter here, Mr. Speaker. This letter contained a small article from the Toronto Telegram, and the person who wrote to me from my constituency told me that this statement is, to his knowledge, absolutely true. I should like to read it:
Hundreds of old age pensioners in Toronto are slowly starving to death-
This may be a sensational statement, but wait until you hear who makes it.
-a Toronto nun claims.
"The public is not aware of the vast number of pensioners suffering from malnutrition," says Sister Mary Vianny, administrator of Providence Villa home for the aged.
"Anyone would find it difficult to live on $75 monthly. More than 250 of the 500 persons at Providence Villa must receive outside help in order to survive on the regular pension."
Speaking at an interfaith rally of the United Appeal, Sister Vianny said that despite government grants in addition to regular pensions, it costs the home more than $20 a month to "give each resident proper care."
She said that Providence Villa was being asked increasingly more to care for pensioners.
"Money is not the only answer," she suggested. "Many older persons living alone do not receive the proper care. They are just sitting in their rooms slowly starving to death."
I believe this to be a statement of fact. I am not putting it forth in sentimental terms because I believe it is a fact. I have called on many of these people and spoken to them. I know that they have this $75 a month. I know that eventually, at some time in the future, through this assistance plan which we are now discussing if the provinces take it up as no doubt they will, these people may be able to get the extra amount they need. But I say that these people are slowly starving to
June 30, 1966

Canada Assistance Plan
death now. These are not my words, they are the words of an experienced social worker speaking to an experienced group.
I could go on and cite other letters of this sort which I have received, but I will not. However, I do have a letter which I think is perhaps typical and it says:
Our government is in trying-
I do not know what that means.
-to solve scandal problems instead of improving legislation such as the old age pension on which the undersigned are dependant upon for a decent existence. We would appreciate it if you could approach the government on our behalf-
This letter is signed by a group of pensioners of the Baron Byng Legion, branch No. 1, Ontario, within my constituency. There are many signatures on it. This being the situation, Mr. Speaker, this is our opportunity to bring to the attention of the government the fact that this is not a political issue or a fictitious issue. This is a real matter affecting people. If we were in a situation in which the required action were impossible to take, then I believe it would be our duty to say so frankly. We would be doing something wrong if we were to hold out hopes that were impossible of fulfilment.
It is not our job, as I understand it, as members of parliament merely to reflect public opinion. If public opinion demanded that something be done that was impossible of fulfilment or would damage the economy of the country, then of course we should say so frankly, whether that was popular or unpopular, and take the consequences of doing so. We are not here merely to reflect opinion, as I understand it, we are here to exercise our judgment on policy. I say, with all the sincerity I can command, it is possible for this affluent country to pay this reasonable amount that is being asked here for all our old age pensioners. I am not going into the economics of the situation. So far as I am concerned, I know that inflation is a serious danger. However, as has been said by my leader, if it is required to impose additional taxation on people, on the well to do and even the less well to do, in order that we may have enough for the old age pensioners to save them from starvation, then I say we should do precisely that. I do not believe there is a single family in my constituency receiving an average income of $5,000 or $6,000 a year who would not pay the extra tax for this sort of thing. But they know very well that some old people perhaps own a home, and out of their pension they may

have to pay $400 taxes. Streetcar fares and the price of bread, milk and rent have been escalating for the old age pensioners. I think I speak for the ordinary people of the country when I say that if it ipeans that the imposition of some extra tax is necessary-and I am not sure it is; I am sure a lot of the cost of an increase would come back in one form or another-the people of this country would accept it as a measure of social justice, and with a willingness to be fair.

I am perfectly prepared to accept that, and I think the people of Canada would be prepared to accept it if they knew the destination of this money and it was shown that a tax was essential. It may well be, with the buoyant revenue received by this government which has produced a boom which is still going on, as I understand it, that we do not need any extra tax. As my leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), said, if there is a danger of inflation, must we take it
June 30, 1966

out on the old age pensioners who can least afford to meet this particular burden?
It was suggested, Mr. Speaker, at one stage of this debate by one or two interrupters on the opposite side of the house, and I think it was repeated in the newspapers-I do not think it was the more thoughtful members opposite who made this suggestion-that we in this part of the house are engaged in some sort of filibuster. I have tried to find out just what is involved in filibustering; it sounds like a nasty and sinister proposition. I found out that a filibuster, according to the definition in the Encyclopaedia of Parliament, 1961, is as follows:
The obstruction of business in a legislature by dilatory tactics, such as speaking merely to consume time. The use of the word in this sense is almost confined to the United States, where the late Senator Huey Long spoke for nearly 16 hours in 1935. He introduced such irrelevancies as recipes for fried oysters and the life of Frederick the Great in a speech alleging an offence by the executive in placing in high-salaried positions men whose names had not been submitted to the Senate for confirmation.
It goes on to say that the United States type of filibustering is not permissible in the House of Commons, and would not be allowed under various standing orders. So that even if I or the members of my party were capable of filibustering, I think we would have difficulty living up to the standards set by Mr. Huey Long.
But, Mr. Speaker, are we filibustering simply because we in this part of the house, faced with what the government itself says is one of its most important measures, and believing that there are gaping deficiencies in it which affect our constituents and people all over Canada, are we to be accused of filibustering because in speaking about this matter we put the needs of our constituents before the house?
I have not been a member of the house for very long, but I do remember sitting here all summer to debate the issue of the Canadian flag. I do not know that I begrudged the time, but I think we spent 30 days on that matter. I think it was an important subject and I do not criticize any member of the house at the time who took part in that debate. But I say that a discussion of a day or two-and a day or two is about all this discussion will occupy-in order to help put before the house what our constituents feel and believe on this question is thoroughly justifiable. I would feel ashamed if I for one had yielded to any suggestion, or if the members of my party had yielded to any suggestion, that we should
Canada Assistance Plan pack up our bags and go home and not talk about these matters at this particular time.
A filibuster is an obstruction of business by people speaking merely to consume time. We are not trying to obstruct business. We expect the Canada Assistance Plan to be passed within a day or two. We do not know that there is any hurry to pass it in the next day or two, but we expect it to be passed. We have made it absolutely clear that, although we think it is inadequate, we do think it is an advance and that it will get our support. But is that any reason that we should be accused in the course of a debate of obstructing the business of the house by filibustering, by speaking to consume time, when we bring before the house the plight of our own constituents in relation to the most important matter in the lives of many of our constituents that we have ever discussed in this house?
Anybody who makes such an accusation, Mr. Speaker, is being blind. It is suggested that it is a terrible thing, that we are holding up the house and do not want to go on a vacation. Personally, I think that that sort of talk is much exaggerated. I know that when the house does recess, as it probably will within a few days, the members of the house will have lots of work to do in their constituencies. I for one would be glad to have the opportunity to get back to my constituency and talk to my constituents about this matter.
I see nothing wrong with our desiring to have a reasonable vacation, in view of the work we do in this house. But to suggest that somebody who wrote an article in a newspaper or some government member leaked the idea that we were to get out by today, and that this would be the last day of this part of the session, and that therefore we are disrupting somebody's plans by insisting on an adequate discussion of the Canada Assistance Plan, is nonsense. We should sit here, if necessary, for as many weeks as are required to deal with this legislation, and to deal, I hope, with the parallel, sister legislation which ought to be introduced. It is clearly the will of the house that legislation dealing with an increase in old age pensions should be introduced. Personally I think that it would be very unfortunate if we in this house were to allow anything to interfere with our responsibilities in this regard.
I have said that the Canada Assistance Plan is a step forward. We have consulted the social workers who see the real advantages in it. We understand that in many fields, as has

June 30. 1966
Canada Assistance Plan been pointed out, the provinces have primary responsibility. But we believe that it is our responsibility in this house to deal with the question of old age pensions, and a minimal way of dealing with it at this time is to increase the pension to $100 a month without a means test. I want to say that in no other subject I have had the opportunity of dealing with in this house in four years am I more conscious of speaking the earnest prayers and desires of my constituents, whether they qualify for old age pension or not.

I give the government and this parliament credit for the Canada Pension Plan. The time will come when this problem may be solved. 1 urge the government to reconsider this matter and to increase pensions, not at some future date, but now, or in the immediate future. I ask the government to yield to the clear will of this house and, I suggest, to the clear will of the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few moments of the time of the house to speak on behalf of the senior citizens in my riding whom it is my honour to represent.
I believe this legislation that has been set before us, known as the Canada Assistance Plan, is one of the greatest pieces of camouflage that we have ever seen in this house. I say that, because it was stated during the election campaign that if the senior citizens would only wait, this government would introduce legislation to be known as the Canada Assistance Plan that would take care of their needs and their wants.
However, I give the minister some credit for this legislation, because it has developed a new concept with respect to welfare work. This legislation has introduced federal assistance for the health care plan, the mothers allowances, child welfare and Indian welfare, also the social welfare workers provision for self training. All these things are good, and I congratulate the minister in tidying up all these welfare acts, which have grown like Topsy, and for bringing them all together under the Canada Assistance Plan.
Whom does this plan assist? It assists most of the people, but it leaves out those very important people who should have assistance, namely the senior citizens. There is no assistance for them whatever. There is not one nickel in this legislation for our senior citizens, unless the provinces agree to enter into the agreement set out with the federal government. It must be remembered that some provinces in Canada are not financially able to enter into this program. What will the senior citizens do in those provinces? The federal government, and not the provincial government, has the responsibility for the senior citizens.
We may take that for granted. What is the senior citizen get that money? He or she application. In your riding, sir, or in my riding we have senior citizens geting $75 a month. You and I know that it is not enough for them to live on, with the great increase in the cost of living. This bill says to them: "But you can get more money". And how does the senior citizen get that money? He or she has to go to the welfare office and, on bended
June 30, 1966

knee, say to the welfare officer:	"Will
you please give me extra money. I cannot live on $75 a month." Our senior citizens have to go begging for that increase.
Is that what this parliament wants our senior citizens to do? That is what is laid down in the bill, as I understand it. It says, in effect: "Go down to the welfare office and ask for a few dollars extra over and above the $75." This was not what was talked about during the election campaign. Now, however, we are faced with facts. This measure is what the government has presented to parliament, asking that it be endorsed.
The members on the other side of the house are not proud of this legislation, they are not satisfied with it. This has been, as members have said, an interesting debate. I think in this country we are going to have to look pretty carefully at welfare programs, and there are areas in which I, for instance, would find myself in quite strong disagreement with the people on my left, geographically and philosophically; but I cannot for the life of me understand the continuing difference of opinion about this particular area of welfare. I refer to the area which has been discussed by the last three or four speakers. I find it hard to see how the

conflicts can be sustained when welfare for our older people-our senior citizens, to use a euphemism-is being discussed.
This is a sector of our population whose capacity for earning is either completely gone or painfully diminished. These are people who, like the rest of us, are living through a period of rapidly rising living costs, and who, because of their own situation, face in addition to the rising cost of living exceptional expenses because of advancing years-the cost of medicine, nursing, special care and transportation. Many of them are no longer able to own or drive a car.
Surely no one in this house or anywhere in Canada has to document the needs of people living today in Canada with the cost of living index where it is, and I am sure it is higher now than it was when I last checked it not too long ago. No one can decently, let alone comfortably, live on $75 a month or $18.75 a week. I do not think that anyone could or would for a moment suggest that this is a proper measure of financial assistance to the older people of this country.
I was much impressed during the last election campaign with the response which the people of my constituency gave to the platform of this party. I suppose no thoughtful member of any party is ever at any time 100 per cent in accord with what his party stands for, but I know that in all the years I have been a member of the Conservative party I have never been more proud of its position than I was in respect of its clear-cut, forthright and consistently retained approach to this problem.
We in this party think that for many reasons the $75 should be forthwith raised to $100. We have said this and, I am happy to say, backed our voices with our votes when this house was seized directly with the question; and for that I am very proud of my membership in this party. This figure should be immediately raised from $75 to $100. I believe that any astute and sensible government would have done so before now.
I am concerned, as I have always been concerned, about the means test, and whether it is euphemistically called a needs test or not does not really alter the case or mitigate my feelings of anxiety about it. The government has said that it has abolished the means test and that what is being used now is a needs test. How is the need established? Is it based on the colour of an old person's eyes or the part of his hair? No, it is established by a most undignified scrutiny into every detail of

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that as a new member I am amazed that the government would wait until this late date to bring before the house such an important piece of legislation. I have to ask myself the question, is it by accident or design that the measure was not placed on the order paper until most members were anxious to get away for a summer recess? Perhaps I am only a frustrated rookie member, but I am afraid I have already reached my own conclusion as to the degree of sincerity behind this legislation. I hope I am wrong and the government will yet take the action that is needed to ensure that our senior citizens will get the relief that is so long overdue and so badly needed. I hope the government will immediately introduce concurrent legislation to increase the old age assistance to $100 a month and reduce the age requirement to 65.

Let me also stress the fact that according to all surveys $100 a month is insufficient. Unless some action is taken now to curb the inflationary cost of living and to provide decent housing within the means of our senior citizens, additional increases in old age assistance will be needed to ensure that these people can enjoy the measure of security they justly deserve. Before I resume my seat, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that perhaps I have been a little naive in answering the many letters requesting relief which I have received from old age pensioners. I have assured them that sooner or later the government would break down and give them the relief that was required. I hope I have not been naive. There will be no one any happier than I if the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) announces there will be concurrent legislation introduced which will give these people the additional increases they require without a needs or means test.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Margaret Rideout (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the course of remarks about the Canada Assistance Plan by hon. members, one theme has tended to recur frequently, namely that the financial needs of the aged should be more adequately recognized, either through an increase in the old age security pension or through the adoption of a guaranteed annual income as recommended in the report of the Senate committee on aging, or in other ways. A number of complimentary references were made to the Senate committee report and it was suggested by some members that the government has not given sufficient attention to its recommendations. I should like, therefore, to devote some attention to that report and to assure you that it has been taken seriously and that action has already been taken on a number of its recommendations. A continued and careful study will be made of the report as a whole.
It should be borne in mind that the Canada Assistance Plan is a measure designed to support the provision of appropriate aid to any person in Canada regardless of his age, place of residence or the cause of his need. Thus, while it provides the basis upon which special attention can be given to particular groups in the country, such as the aged, it nevertheless helps to assure that the needs of all groups will be considered. Indeed, it is only through the development of very comprehensive and soundly conceived assistance
June 30, 1966

measures for the total population that the needs of particular groups can be adequately met.
This approach is recognized by the Senate committee on aging and is set out as the first principle for relating this approach to the needs of the aged. I quote from page 7 of the report as follows:
1.	The welfare of older people is closely linked with the welfare of all Canadians. Many of the problems older people face are the result of new developments in society, such as rapid technological change, which are having their effects on other age groups as well. This means that constructive planning for old people cannot proceed on an ad hoc basis, but must rest on an analysis and understanding of the social situation.
2.	Society has a responsibility to protect and assist disadvantaged groups in the population, such as older people under present day conditions, but in doing so must also take account of the wider public interest.
Commencing with this realistic approach to social need, the report of the Senate committee goes on to make a number of recommendations which, in its opinion, must be implemented if our society is to fully accept its responsibilities toward its older citizens. The first of these, and the one which has received the greatest attention, concerns the need for income security. Specifically, the recommendation is that an income guarantee program should be established. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) has already stated to this house that this proposal is being carefully considered, but that there are important implications which were not brought out in the Senate report which must be considered before any responsible decision can be taken. This view is held also by the Canadian Welfare Council, which has established a sound reputation as a responsible and well informed spokesman for the views of social welfare in Canada.
In a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) dated May 29, 1966, the council makes the following statement:
The council believes that the principle of a guaranteed income for the aged has much to commend it. However, there are many questions that should be studied, and related decisions made, before a conclusion is reached as to whether such a program should be undertaken. These questions are concerned with the proposal itself, and with current and future programs to improve the living standards not only of the aged but of all Canada's needy people.
The council sets out seven major questions which in its opinion need to be answered before a decision is reached. These are as follows:
1. Has parliament the constitutional power to institute an income guarantee program?
Canada Assistance Plan
2 What priority should be given to the economic needs of the elderly vis-5-vis those of the rest of the population (recent studies carried out by the Canadian Welfare Council have shown that a relatively large proportion of the total population is living in poverty, many below the present level of the old age security pension).
3.	Should a guaranteed income program as recommended for the aged also apply to the blind and disabled?
4.	What would be the impact of a guaranteed income on the incentive built into the Canada Pension Plan to keep people 65 to 70 years of age in the labour force?
5.	If such a program were inaugurated:
(a)	What would constitute "income" for purposes of calculating the deficiency between what income a claimant has and what he should receive?
(b)	How would the amount of the guaranteed income be determined and what devices would be necessary to keep it abreast of the standard of living?
(c)	Would the guaranteed income be the same across Canada or would there be regional differences?
(d)	What provision would be made for dependent spouses (under 65) and children, when the beneficiary is alive and when he or she dies?
(e)	On what basis would an applicant's first year benefits be calculated?
(f)	How would overpayments be dealt with?
6.	What are the alternatives to such a program?
7.	Should a sickness cash benefit program be established for all people with or without an income guarantee?
The Senate committee, in putting forward this recommendation, recognized that it had not been in the position to estimate the cost of an income guaranteed program, and suggested that the proposal should be given immediate study.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has already stated that through the Canada Assistance Plan the federal government will contribute toward the cost of providing assistance to older persons whose income is insufficient to meet their needs.
[DOT] ( 5:40 p.m.)
He pointed out that no ceiling is set on the amount of the federal contribution and that the concept of assistance is sufficiently broad to cover any element of need that may be present. It includes, for example, the cost of a comprehensive range of health care services, the lack of which represents one of the most costly and worrying problems facing older people today. It includes institutional care and a variety of welfare services to which I will shortly refer in greater detail. It is anticipated that the substantial federal funds to be made available to the provinces will contribute materially to their ability to provide the additional assistance to all older persons who require it.

June 30. 1966
Canada Assistance Plan
I would now like to refer to other recommendations that appear in the Senate committee's report. There are in all 92 recommendations under seven headings, covering the general topics of income status and security, employment status and opportunities, health status and health care, housing status and needs, community services for old people, research and statistics, and planning and co-ordination. Many of the recommendations come within the area of responsibility of other government departments, where they are being given close attention.
I can take the time to list only a few of the recommendations that come within the fields of health and welfare. The following illustrate the range of needs to be covered, and you will note in some instances refer specifically to the Canada Assistance Plan.
Home care programs for the elderly should be greatly extended. They should include medical and nursing care, physiotherapy and other rehabilitative services, and visiting homemakers.
Counselling services provided by local welfare departments to the elderly and others should be a shareable cost under the Canada Assistance Plan.
Municipalities should extend counselling services for old people and develop foster home placement services.
Homemaker services should be accepted as a shareable cost under the Canada Assistance Plan.
Study should be given by the appropriate authority to the place and function of homes for the aged, and in particular attention should be given to prevailing admission policies, the possibility of alternative accommodation in sheltered semi-independent housing for relatively well ambulant patients, the placing of rehabilitation or "reactivization" programs, and the careful selection and training of staff.
Grants under the health and welfare training programs of the federal government should be used to increase the supply of workers equipped for work in the field of old age.
The welfare branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare should establish a specific division for the purpose of providing technical advice and up-to-date information with regard to day care centres, homemakers, meal services, counselling and such other welfare services for the elderly as come within its terms of reference.

The Senate report clearly documents the need for the variety of social welfare services proposed, and indicates that, to the extent to which they are provided, older people can be helped to maintain their independence as fully and as long as possible. The Canada Assistance Plan has been specifically designed to give emphasis to the general approach put forward by the Senate committee, but in doing so includes the needs of the total population along with the needs of that particularly deserving group, the aged.
Let me list some examples of services provided for under the plan, and relate them to the aged. First, health care services, including not only medical, surgical and optical and nursing services, but also such important items as drugs and prosthetic appliances. Hon. members will know that one of the more costly items required by many older people is that of drugs, and the federal contribution toward this item alone will help to alleviate the concerns of older people who are presently unable to meet the high cost of medication.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the hon. member continues would she allow a question. She has mentioned the question of drugs and the alleviation of the conditions under which so many old people, as well as other people, operate owing to the high cost of drugs. Is she aware of the fact that a request has come from the government of Saskatchewan for the immediate removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on drugs, and what is the attitude of the government in that regard?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the right hon. gentleman's question but I will say only this at the moment. I think he is probably well aware that the committee on the cost of food and drugs is still hearing witnesses and certainly is concerned, as is the right hon. gentleman, about a most important matter.
Second, homes for special care and particularly homes for the aged and nursing homes. Federal contributions will be available not only to help cover the costs of care in such homes, but also of the important services that should be attached to them. I refer here to such services as physiotherapy, occupational therapy and nursing services. In this connection I might also note that federal contributions may be made available toward the cost of day care services which may be set up in conjunction with an institution or separately.
June 30/ 1966

Through such services older people can remain in their own homes but at the same time receive the attention provided in a day care setting.
Third, homemaker services. Particular attention was given by the Senate committee to the importance of homemaker services through which older persons, in their own homes, can be assisted and supported and provided with the help and care needed to enable them to carry on independently and to postpone, as long as possible, the need to enter an institution.
Fourth, counselling services. The Senate committee report also emphasized the importance of various forms of counselling services through which older persons can be given advice and help where needed and can be referred to appropriate services in a community. The plan provides for federal contributions in this respect as well as for other rehabilitation services required by the aged.
In addition to providing for federal contributions toward the costs of providing assistance and welfare services, the bill provides for the Department of National Health and Welfare to make consultative services available to the provinces with respect to the development and operation of assistance and welfare services programs. There are already consultants on the staff of the department, and others will be appointed as soon as qualified persons can be recruited. Particular attention is being and will continue to be paid to the needs of the aged.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
May I also say, Mr. Speaker, the Canada Assistance Plan provides a sound basis for the development, extension and improvement of assistance and welfare services for the aged. It acknowledges and provides for the wide variety of needs that older persons face. It contributes toward the research and evaluation needed to assess and develop services in accordance with changing needs. It contributes to the cost of training the skilled personnel required to provide the services. It takes into account the representations put forward by the many organizations who speak for the aged, and represents a major step forward in ensuring that our older citizens can have access to the help needed to enable them to live full, independent and satisfying lives.
If I might, Mr. Speaker, I should like for a few moments to speak about the child welfare program as it is covered in the Canada 23033-450a
Canada Assistance Plan Assistance Plan. I am sure that all hon. members who have children, as I have, recognize the special care that is needed for the children who are in need, unwanted and uncared for. I wish to take a few moments of the time of the house to speak of this particular aspect of the Canada Assistance Plan which is very near and dear to my heart.
Hon. members will have observed that the plan covers persons under the age of 21 who are in the care or custody or under the control or supervision of a child welfare authority, or who are foster children-that is, children in receipt of assistance but not under the supervision of child welfare agencies.
I understand that some 50,000 children are in the care of child welfare agencies in Canada. The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Enns), a social worker himself with years of experience in charge of an important child welfare agency, emphasized in the speech I mentioned earlier that "one of the difficulties in the welfare structure is the inadequacy of the provision for children," and went on to say: "I must point out that child welfare services have been understaffed all across the land." He knows what he is talking about.
Fifty thousand children. And these are not all that are being helped by child welfare agencies. For example, I believe that something like 13,000 children are placed for adoption each year by our child welfare services in Canada. Still others need placement, and adoption homes might be found for them if more trained staff could be employed.
It has often been pointed out by child welfare agencies that many children who come into their care might have been able to stay in their own homes, or be returned to them without undue delay, if the agencies could provide adequate family rehabilitative services, which all too frequently is not possible because of limited funds. I quote again from the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa who, in referring to child welfare agencies, remarked that: "Those agencies are provided the rehabilitative services concerned with the basic unit in Canadian society-namely, the family" and he indicated that these services were in urgent need of being strengthened. Saving or restoring the family for the child is sound social policy and makes sense from an economic point of view. Here is one place where those who are concerned with the welfare of people and those whose chief interest is in saving money may find themselves on common ground.

June 30, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan
This leads me to the important concept of prevention which is a basic feature of the Canada Assistance Plan. We have heard of the dependency cycle and the need to break it at some point. Well, what better point than that of the child. Later may be too late, despite our best efforts. But our success at the point of the child is dependant upon the skill and knowledge to be found in our child welfare agencies and the resources available to them. The Canada Assistance Plan will encourage the development of better services to children and the expansion of resources available to child welfare agencies, such as day-care, homemakers, adoption, casework and other services.
Lately, I have read in the newspapers about the inadequacies in the number of facilities in some provinces for the special care of emotionally disturbed children. Many of these children do not require hospital treatment. What they need is a type of non-medical special care which normally comes under welfare auspices. This is provided in a number of institutions across Canada, some being former orphanages which have now developed specialized programs for this type of child. These would be covered under the plan.
There are other children who may suffer disturbances and may need treatment under medical auspices, and there are still others whose needs are for correctional care or better educational facilities. Provision for these types of need lies outside the scope of the Canada Assistance Plan and belongs elsewhere.
However, the better the job that is done by the child welfare services, including the special care for emotionally disturbed children, the less need there will be for hospital treatment and correctional facilities for children and, I might add, for adults. I believe it makes good sense to aid in the development of these vitally needed services.
The integration of child welfare into a comprehensive welfare plan for all Canadians is a step forward and basic to a fully-rounded program designed to help meet the needs of people. The coverage by the Canada Assistance Plan of children who are in need of social assistance and welfare services complements the federal government's existing income support measures for children-namely, family allowances, family assistance-that is, the family allowance program for children from abroad during their first year in Canada-and youth allowances.
tMrs. Rideout.]
I have attempted to point up the various ways in which the Canada Assistance Plan supports the provision of assistance and welfare services for children, and I am sure that hon. members will agree that federal funds devoted to this purpose will be well spent. But the Canada Assistance Plan is also an integrating measure. Up to now, child welfare services have been largely provided by agencies or departments which direct their entire attention to children. This focus can now be shifted and attention given to the needs of children as members of a family unit, with the objective of helping to keep families together and prevent the need for the care of children outside their own homes.
The close integration of child welfare with public assistance and its related welfare services is an objective which has been advocated by all provinces. It represents a major step forward in ensuring that the needs of people of all ages can be properly and effectively met.
